15.2 Double Integrals over General Regions

From rectangles to any bounded region : put inside a rectangle, use a function that is zero outside , and get iterated integrals for Type I and Type II regions. Then two worked examples (one needs the order of integration reversed), the six properties of double integrals, and an estimate that uses nothing but the smallest and largest values of .

Definition

As long as the boundary of is “well-behaved”, then exists.

Explanation (added)

Why this works. Every box over a part of outside has height , so it adds nothing to the Riemann sum. Only the boxes over count, and there . So collects exactly what should mean. It also does not matter which rectangle you pick: a bigger only adds more zero-height boxes.

Why “well-behaved”. usually jumps from down to along the boundary of (the cliff in the picture), so is not continuous on . The integral still exists when is continuous on and the boundary curve is reasonable (the curves in this course always are). Stewart §15.2 says the same and leaves the precise condition out of the book.

3Type II regions: between and

The same idea with the roles of and swapped: lies between a left curve and a right curve, and the strips are horizontal.

Type II regions:

In green on the board:

Board slip: this set is the Type II region , not the rectangle . It should read . The rectangle is , as in the sketch.

Explanation (added)

The reasons are the Type I reasons with and swapped: use Fubini on with inside, then notice that for a fixed , is only for and otherwise along the horizontal line. The green brace marks the inner integral: its limits depend on only, so they are constants while you integrate in .

How to tell which type you have. Draw a vertical line through : if it always enters through the same bottom curve and leaves through the same top curve, is Type I. Draw a horizontal line: if it always enters through the same left curve and leaves through the same right curve, is Type II. Many regions are both (all four examples in the widget below are Type I; three are also Type II without splitting).

Explanation (added)

What went wrong in the crossed-out attempt. It swapped to and kept the limits where they were. But in the outer integral has the limit , and has already been integrated out, so the result would still contain . That is why the circled limits are the warning sign: the outer limits must be constants, and the inner limits may depend only on the outer variable. The limits cannot be moved around; they have to be read off the region again.

Reading the region. The given limits say and : horizontal strips from the line to . That is the triangle in the sketch. Described with vertical strips: goes from to , and at each , goes from the -axis up to the line, .

Why the new order helps. Now the inner integral is in , where is a constant, so it gives , and the limits and leave the factor . That is exactly what needs (). The -limits are and , the same numbers as before.

6Properties of double integrals, 1–4

The rules you used for single integrals carry over. Property 4 is the new useful one: cut into pieces and add.

Properties of Double Integrals

Assuming all integrals exist:

  3. If for all , then
  4. If and or is just the shared boundary of and , then

In the top-right corner of the board, the one-variable version of Property 4:

– Useful if isn’t type I or II, but we decompose it so each piece is.

Explanation (added)

1 and 2 say a double integral is linear, exactly like a single integral: constants come out, and the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals. 3 is comparison: a taller surface over the same region has at least as much (signed) volume under it. In particular, if on then , which is the check used in Section 4.

4 is the corner sketch one dimension up. The pieces may share boundary curves, because a curve has no area and adds nothing to the integral. This is how to handle a region where one formula does not describe the whole top, bottom, left or right side: cut it where the formula changes. In the strip widget in Section 3, the region between and is a single Type I region but needs two pieces as a Type II region, split at .

The lecture’s results

What a typical exam question looks like
  1. Evaluate over a region bounded by curves. Find where the curves meet, sketch , decide whether it is Type I or Type II (or which is less work), write the limits and integrate (Sections 2–4).
  2. Reverse the order of integration. An iterated integral whose inner integral has no elementary antiderivative, like , , or : sketch the region, switch the order, evaluate (Section 5).
  3. Sketch the region of a given iterated integral, or rewrite it with the order reversed without evaluating it.
  4. Volume or area. The volume under above a region bounded by curves, or the area of as (Sections 4 and 7).
  5. Split a region that is not Type I or Type II in one piece, using Property 4 (Section 6).
  6. Estimate with Property 6: bound on by hand and multiply by the area of (Section 8).

Tests are written without a calculator, so answers stay exact, like , or .
